title: Understand the basic practices of beekeeping and the benefit thereof for agriculture

lessons.title: Bees, nectar, pollen and propolis
lessons.html:
Why bees matter to farmers

Honey bees make honey, but their biggest gift to farming is pollination. When a bee visits flowers, it carries pollen from one flower to another. This helps the flower make fruit and seed. Crops such as apples, pears, avocados, macadamias, berries, pumpkins, sunflowers and lucerne seed need or benefit from bees. Many South African fruit farmers hire beehives during flowering.

South Africa has two honey bee types: the Cape honey bee in the south-west and the African honey bee in the rest of the country.

Where bee food comes from

  • Nectar: a sweet liquid made in flowers to attract insects. Bees suck it up and turn it into honey. Honey is the bees' energy food.
  • Pollen: the fine yellow, orange or white powder in flowers. Bees carry it home in "baskets" on their back legs. It is their protein food, fed to young bees.
  • Propolis: a sticky resin that bees collect from tree buds and bark. They use it to seal cracks in the hive and keep it clean, because it fights germs.

How plants make these products

Plants make sugar in their leaves using sunlight, water and air. Some of this sugar goes into nectar. Pollen is made in the male parts of the flower (the anthers). Resin is made by some trees to protect their buds and wounds.

Bee safety

  • Bees sting to protect their hive. Keep calm and walk away from a hive; do not swat bees.
  • If many bees attack, cover your face and move quickly to a building or vehicle.
  • Scrape a sting out with a fingernail or card.
  • Some people have a severe allergic reaction: swelling of the face and throat, breathing trouble. This is an emergency; get medical help immediately.
  • Only trained beekeepers in protective suits should open hives.

lessons.title: The environment and bee plants
lessons.html:
How the environment affects nectar and pollen

Plants do not always give the same amount of nectar and pollen. It changes with:

  • Rain and soil moisture: in drought, plants make little nectar or stop flowering.
  • Temperature: very cold or very hot weather reduces nectar. Bees also fly less in cold, wet or windy weather.
  • Wind: dries out nectar and keeps bees in the hive.
  • Soil fertility: healthy plants on good soil give more flowers.
  • Time of day: many flowers give nectar in the morning.
  • Pesticides: sprays during flowering can kill bees. Farmers should spray when bees are not flying, use products that are less harmful to bees, and warn beekeepers before spraying.
  • Fire and land clearing: destroy bee plants.

Important bee plants in South Africa

PlantWhat it gives bees
Eucalyptus (gum trees)Important nectar and pollen source for beekeepers in many areas
CitrusNectar; well-known orange blossom honey
SunflowerNectar and pollen in summer
CanolaNectar and pollen in the Western Cape
Lucerne and cloversNectar
AloesWinter nectar and pollen when little else flowers
Fynbos plantsNectar and pollen for the Cape honey bee
Acacias and other indigenous treesPollen and nectar; resin for propolis from some trees

A good bee area has different plants flowering at different times of the year, so bees always have food. When there is a gap with no flowers, colonies get weak and beekeepers may have to move hives or feed the bees.

Some gum tree species are invasive and are controlled by law in certain areas, so beekeepers and farmers need to plan forage carefully.

lessons.title: Beekeeping practices and the potential of bee plants
lessons.html:
Basic beekeeping practices

  • The hive: most beekeepers use wooden Langstroth boxes with frames. The bottom box (brood chamber) holds the queen and young bees; the top boxes (supers) hold honey.
  • The colony: one queen lays eggs; thousands of female worker bees collect food and care for the hive; male drones mate with queens.
  • Siting hives: near water and bee plants, away from houses, roads and kraals, with shade in summer, on stands to keep ants and water out.
  • Inspection: trained beekeepers wear a bee suit, veil, gloves and boots, and use a smoker to calm the bees.
  • Harvesting honey: only from the supers, leaving enough honey for the bees.
  • Health: watch for pests such as wax moth and small hive beetle, and diseases. Report unusual bee deaths.

The potential of bee plants for the farm

  • Pollination gives better fruit set, bigger and better-shaped fruit, and higher seed yields.
  • Extra income: honey, wax, pollen and propolis can be sold, or hives rented out for pollination.
  • Planting bee plants such as aloes, indigenous trees and flowering cover crops on farm edges gives bees food all year, especially when crops are not flowering.
  • Healthy environment: protecting natural veld and fynbos supports wild bees and other pollinators too.

What workers can do

  • Do not disturb hives or wild nests; report them to your supervisor.
  • Follow spraying instructions that protect bees.
  • Do not burn or cut flowering plants unnecessarily.
  • Keep water troughs with a floating plank so bees can drink without drowning.

Key points

  • Bees pollinate many crops, giving more and better fruit and seed.
  • Nectar is energy food, pollen is protein food and propolis seals and cleans the hive.
  • Rain, temperature, wind and pesticides change how much food plants give bees.
  • Important SA bee plants include gums, citrus, sunflower, canola, aloes and fynbos.
  • Stay calm near bees; severe allergic reactions are an emergency.
